body.text: U.S. foreign policy has entered a period of uncertainty. Democrats swept to power in both the Senate and the House on November 3, meaning that President Donald Trump will lose control of Congress two years before he leaves office.

In Foreign Affairs, Daniel Drezner and Elizabeth Saunders warned that a lame-duck Trump would be most dangerous where he can act on his own, such as by escalating in Iran or Cuba. They are right about the danger. But what a lame-duck president can still do is only one side of the equation. The other side is whether other governments and leaders still want to deal with Trump.

Later this week, the presidents of the United States and China will meet again, but in a multilateral setting rather than a summit of their own making. It’s their third meeting in 2026 following bilateral summits in May and September, the first of which some read as a sign that a China-U.S. influence transition is underway.

Post-midterm summits can still be a boon for presidents wounded politically at home. Bill Clinton attended the APEC summit in Indonesia after the 1994 election, George W. Bush flew to APEC in Hanoi a week after losing Congress in 2006, and Barack Obama traveled to Asia after losing the midterms in 2010. Foreign travel, as Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, put it last week, is “something that no domestic opposition can do.” Summitry is an arena where a president is largely free to act and bring home results.

Yet there is a catch. Clinton faced skeptical Asian economic partners as he pushed for an agreement on open and free trade; Bush faced tests by Asian allies over the North Korean threat and the rise of China; and Obama, touring Asian democracies in a tacit challenge to China’s economic model, left Seoul without the South Korea-U.S. trade deal he had sought. Congress cannot follow Trump to Asia, but foreign leaders, who follow other countries’ domestic politics closely, have watched the U.S. midterms closely. The summit circuit may allow a president to escape his domestic critics, but often brings him into contact with a tougher foreign audience.

The president who built his brand on contempt for multilateralism will spend his first post-midterm weeks in multilateral meetings: the ASEAN–U.S. summit and the first Quad leaders’ meeting in two years, both in Manila, then the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, and in December the G-20 at his own resort in Miami. Trump is still the diplomat-in-chief. But these summits are better read as a stage on which the rest of the world will show how much his words still matter.

Multilateral summits are rarely remembered for their own sake. The communiques are drafted in advance and forgotten soon after. The real value of multilateral summits is what takes place on the sidelines: who asks to meet whom, who gets a meeting, and who is left waiting.

The unscripted moments between formal sessions, when leaders interact and socialize, can reveal just as much. An influential great power is one whose leader others line up to see. Leaders will still meet Trump; what matters is who seeks him out and who queues up to meet China’s President Xi Jinping or Premier Li Qiang first.

This week, we will get an immediate test of how Asian partners, many of them hit by Washington’s tariffs, treat a weakened president. What meetings will Trump hold, and can Washington still turn those summits into progress on its own agenda? And how will Beijing use its role as host of the APEC summit to advance its own priorities?
The Manila Summits: ASEAN and the Quad

Since last year, the United States has imposed tariffs on allies and rivals alike. In response, most governments have chosen accommodation. Japan pledged $550 billion in investment; South Korea similarly promised $350 billion. But concessions made to a president with two years left in office and a hostile Congress mean less than they once did. Partners now want to know whether their deals with Trump will outlast him.

The region’s mood is less defiant than anxious. Japan has been jittery since the midterms, and Tokyo fears being sidelined in a U.S. deal with China, Russia, or North Korea. The three-way meeting with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen is exactly the sort of diplomacy that gives Japanese leaders nightmares. South Korea is meanwhile working to minimize the impact of the midterm election on its security deals with the United States.

Some hedging is a given, and it will show up in the meeting schedules. Some leaders will ask for time with Trump, some with Xi, and some with both. For those leaders who do meet with Trump, some may offer him new concessions while others simply pose for a handshake.

The summits in Manila will offer an important indication of whether Washington can still turn access into results. The Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings. As an added advantage for Trump, China customarily sends its premier, not Xi, to the ASEAN conclave.

In Manila, the Trump administration hopes to close trade deals and persuade Southeast Asian governments to build on American AI technology in exchange for development aid. Washington also hopes to use the Quad summit to repair strained ties with India. Delhi was due to host the Quad summit last year, but did not, due to the ongoing tariff disputes with Washington.

Trump’s stop in Manila will be brief. He is scheduled to land after the East Asia Summit has begun for an ASEAN–U.S. meeting, a Quad summit, and a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. If Southeast Asian leaders line up to see him and sign on to his technology agenda, and if the Quad delivers, the lame duck still has pull. Expectations, however, are modest.
The APEC Summit in Shenzhen

Right after the ASEAN meetings, Trump will travel to Shenzhen. The White House has described Trump’s meeting with Xi there as “a short, a routine visit,” unlike their major bilateral summits in May and September. Under Trump, APEC has never been a priority. He skipped it in 2018, and last year he left the summit in Gyeongju before the leaders’ meeting began, right after a one-on-one meeting with Xi in Busan.

For China, by contrast, APEC has been an important means of integrating its economy into the global economy since it joined in 1991. When Trump skipped the leaders’ summit last year, Xi used the empty chair to cast China as the defender of free trade, a role that the United States used to play.

Trump is not going to Shenzhen for APEC. He is going for Xi, and for the three-way meeting with Putin he hopes to hold on denuclearization and Iran. Beijing, however, gets to decide how the trilateral is staged. For decades, foreign leaders came to summits hoping for time with the U.S. president. In Shenzhen, Trump come looking for time with Xi and Putin.

Washington is seeking progress on short-term foreign policy goals that will address Trump’s domestic political vulnerabilities: an exit from the war in Iran and an arms-control agreement with Russia. For Beijing, the APEC summit is about rules that will serve its interests in the longer term. China has used its year as APEC chair to revive the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific and to promote open trade and resilient supply chains, which it has contrasted with U.S. protectionism. These goals are meant to outlast any single U.S. president.

Xi skipped the G-20 in 2023 and 2025 but has kept coming to APEC, and this year he is the host. China’s diplomatic pull is undeniable. Putin is planning to come to Shenzhen for his first in-person attendance at APEC since 2017, but is expected to skip the G-20 in Miami.

At the same time, hosting comes with risks. In 2018, APEC leaders failed to issue a joint declaration for the first time, after Washington and Beijing clashed on trade and investment. To call the Shenzhen summit a success China will need to meet four goals: produce a consensus statement after the APEC summit, advance regional free trade, stage the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting on its own terms, and draw serious engagement from the United States’ allies and partners.
A Transition Moment

Trump’s May summit with Xi yielded little beyond a vague commitment on Iran, yet some hailed it as a shift in power. September’s meeting in Washington, D.C., was widely seen as a stalemate that flattered Beijing. But those were bilateral encounters, staged by the two parties. Whether the China-U.S. influence transition is indeed in progress, and whether others accept it, is another matter. The summits this week – the first multilateral meetings featuring both Trump and Xi since their bilateral in May – will provide our first clue. If Washington’s partners lean toward Beijing, Trump’s agenda stalls in Manila, and China hosts APEC with authority, the transition will become visible to the rest of the world.

There are reasons for caution. China’s economy is slowing, and Beijing has ongoing issues with its neighbors, such as the South China Sea disputes, where negotiations on the Code of Conduct remain unfinished. But China needs only to look steadier than Washington, and in a lame-duck period in the United States following two years of tumultuous U.S. foreign policy that is a low bar.

If leaders line up for Xi in Shenzhen, Washington still has a chance to answer with the G-20 summit in Miami. An early signal will be whether Xi travels there at all; he’s skipped two of the last three G-20 summits, sending Li Qiang in his place to the summits in 2023 and 2025.
If leaders still line up to talk to Trump in Manila and Shenzhen, talk of a power shift will look premature.

Drezner and Saunders are right that a lame duck is dangerous because of what he can still do alone. But any world leader’s power is in part determined by the response from his foreign counterparts. That will be on display this week in the meeting schedules and sideline encounters, not to mention whether Trump comes home with any substantial agreements.
